subject: Biology
title: Reproduction
outline: Compare asexual and sexual reproduction and give examples
Describe the cell cycle, mitosis and meiosis and state their significance
Describe the structure of a flower, pollination, fertilisation and fruit/seed formation
Describe the human reproductive systems, menstrual cycle, fertilisation and development
Explain metamorphosis and reproduction in other animals
Discuss birth control, family planning and reproductive health

modules.title: Cell Division: Mitosis and Meiosis
modules.html:
1. The Cell Cycle

Interphase (G₁, S — DNA replication, G₂) occupies most of the cycle and is followed by the mitotic phase (karyokinesis then cytokinesis).

2. Mitosis

Mitosis produces two daughter cells genetically identical to the parent, each with the same chromosome number (diploid remains diploid).

  1. Prophase – chromosomes condense and appear as two chromatids joined at a centromere; nuclear membrane and nucleolus disappear; spindle forms.
  2. Metaphase – chromosomes line up singly at the equator, attached to spindle fibres.
  3. Anaphase – centromeres divide; chromatids are pulled to opposite poles.
  4. Telophase – chromosomes decondense; nuclear membranes reform; cytokinesis follows (cleavage furrow in animals, cell plate in plants).

Significance: growth, repair and replacement of tissues, asexual reproduction and genetic stability.

3. Meiosis

Meiosis is a reduction division of two successive stages (meiosis I and II) producing four haploid daughter cells from one diploid cell:

$$2n \rightarrow n$$
  • In prophase I homologous chromosomes pair (synapsis) forming bivalents; crossing over at chiasmata exchanges genetic material.
  • In metaphase I the bivalents line up and independent assortment occurs; anaphase I separates whole homologues.
  • Meiosis II resembles mitosis and separates the chromatids.

Significance: halves the chromosome number so that fertilisation restores the diploid number, and creates genetic variation through crossing over and independent assortment.

MitosisMeiosis
One division, 2 cellsTwo divisions, 4 cells
Chromosome number retainedChromosome number halved
Daughter cells identicalDaughter cells genetically different
Somatic (body) cellsGamete-forming (germ) cells

examples.q: A cell with 24 chromosomes undergoes meiosis. State the number of cells produced and the chromosome number of each.
examples.a: Four cells are produced, each with 12 chromosomes, because meiosis is a reduction division: \( 2n = 24 \rightarrow n = 12 \).

examples.q: Explain two ways in which meiosis creates variation.
examples.a: (i) Crossing over at chiasmata during prophase I exchanges segments between homologous chromosomes, producing new gene combinations. (ii) Independent assortment at metaphase I means each pair of homologues can line up in either orientation, giving \(2^n\) possible gamete combinations.

modules.title: Reproduction in Plants
modules.html:
1. Asexual Reproduction

  • Binary fission (Amoeba, bacteria), budding (yeast, Hydra), fragmentation (Spirogyra), spore formation (Rhizopus, ferns).
  • Vegetative propagation: stem tuber (Irish potato), rhizome (ginger), corm (cocoyam), bulb (onion), runner (grass), sucker (banana), and artificial methods — cutting, layering, grafting, budding, tissue culture.

Advantages: rapid, no mate required, offspring identical to a good parent. Disadvantages: no variation, overcrowding, disease may wipe out the whole clone.

2. The Flower

PartFunction
Calyx (sepals)Protects the bud
Corolla (petals)Attracts pollinators (in insect-pollinated flowers)
Androecium (stamens: anther + filament)Produces pollen grains (male gametes)
Gynoecium (carpel: stigma, style, ovary)Receives pollen; ovary contains ovules

3. Pollination

Pollination is the transfer of pollen from anther to stigma; it is self- or cross-pollination. Cross-pollination is favoured by dioecy, protandry, protogyny, heterostyly and self-sterility, and produces more vigorous, variable offspring.

Insect-pollinatedWind-pollinated
Large, brightly coloured, scented petals with nectarSmall, dull, no scent or nectar
Sticky or spiky pollen, moderate amountLight, smooth pollen in large quantity
Anthers and stigma enclosedAnthers and feathery stigma exposed and pendulous

4. Fertilisation and Fruit Formation

The pollen grain germinates, and the pollen tube grows down the style guided by chemotropism. Double fertilisation occurs: one male nucleus fuses with the egg cell to form the diploid zygote, the other with the two polar nuclei to give the triploid endosperm. Afterwards the ovule becomes the seed, the integuments become the testa, and the ovary becomes the fruit. Fruits and seeds are dispersed by wind, water, animals or explosive mechanisms.

examples.q: Give three adaptations of a wind-pollinated flower.
examples.a: (i) Long filaments hold versatile anthers outside the flower so pollen is caught by the wind. (ii) Large feathery stigmas hang out to trap airborne pollen. (iii) Pollen grains are small, light, smooth and produced in very large numbers, compensating for wastage.

examples.q: State the products of double fertilisation in an angiosperm.
examples.a: A diploid zygote (2n), which develops into the embryo, and a triploid primary endosperm nucleus (3n), which forms the nutritive endosperm tissue of the seed.

modules.title: Reproduction in Humans and Other Animals
modules.html:
1. Reproductive Systems

Male: testes in the scrotum (sperm and testosterone), epididymis, vas deferens, seminal vesicle, prostate and Cowper’s glands (seminal fluid), urethra and penis.
Female: ovaries (ova and hormones), oviducts (Fallopian tubes — site of fertilisation), uterus, cervix and vagina.

2. The Menstrual Cycle (about 28 days)

  1. Days 1–5: menstruation — the uterine lining is shed.
  2. Days 6–13: FSH stimulates a Graafian follicle; oestrogen repairs and thickens the endometrium.
  3. Day 14: LH surge causes ovulation.
  4. Days 15–28: the corpus luteum secretes progesterone, maintaining the lining. If fertilisation does not occur the corpus luteum degenerates, progesterone falls and menstruation begins again.

3. Fertilisation, Pregnancy and Birth

Fertilisation in the oviduct forms a zygote which divides by mitosis to a morula and blastocyst, then implants in the uterine wall. The placenta allows exchange of oxygen, nutrients, antibodies and waste between maternal and fetal blood without the two mixing, and secretes progesterone. The amnion and amniotic fluid protect the fetus from shock, dehydration and temperature change. Gestation lasts about 280 days and ends with labour, driven by oxytocin.

4. Reproduction in Other Animals

  • Fish and amphibians: external fertilisation, many eggs, little parental care.
  • Reptiles and birds: internal fertilisation, shelled amniotic eggs, oviparous.
  • Insects: complete metamorphosis (egg → larva → pupa → adult, as in butterfly, housefly, mosquito) or incomplete metamorphosis (egg → nymph → adult, as in grasshopper, cockroach).

5. Family Planning and Reproductive Health

Methods include natural (rhythm/safe period, abstinence), barrier (condom, diaphragm), chemical (spermicides), hormonal (pills, injections, implants), intra-uterine devices and surgical (vasectomy, tubal ligation). Benefits: child spacing, reduced maternal and infant mortality, better family welfare and control of population growth. Condoms additionally reduce transmission of HIV and other sexually transmitted infections.

examples.q: In a regular 28-day cycle, when is ovulation most likely and why is it important in family planning?
examples.a: Ovulation occurs about day 14, roughly 14 days before the next menstruation. Since sperm can survive up to 5 days and the ovum about 24 hours, the fertile window is about days 9–16. The rhythm method depends on avoiding intercourse during this period, but it is unreliable in women with irregular cycles.

Complete metamorphosis has four stages — egg, larva, pupa, adult — and the larva differs completely from the adult in form and diet (butterfly, mosquito). Incomplete metamorphosis has three stages — egg, nymph, adult — with the nymph resembling a small wingless adult and sharing its habitat and food (grasshopper, cockroach).

quiz.q: The type of cell division that produces gametes is
quiz.solution: Meiosis halves the chromosome number to form haploid gametes.

quiz.q: During which stage of mitosis do chromatids move to opposite poles?
quiz.solution: The centromeres divide and spindle fibres pull the chromatids apart in anaphase.
Homologous chromosomes pair and exchange segments at chiasmata in prophase I.

quiz.q: A diploid cell with 20 chromosomes produces gametes containing
quiz.solution: Meiosis halves the number, so each gamete has 10 chromosomes.

quiz.q: Which is an example of vegetative propagation by an underground stem?
quiz.solution: The ginger rhizome is a horizontal underground stem bearing buds.

quiz.q: A major disadvantage of asexual reproduction is
quiz.solution: Genetically identical offspring are equally vulnerable to the same disease or change.

quiz.q: The male gametes of a flowering plant are contained in the
quiz.solution: Pollen grains contain the generative nucleus which divides into two male nuclei.

quiz.q: Which feature indicates that a flower is wind pollinated?
quiz.solution: Large feathery stigmas project into the air to trap airborne pollen.

quiz.q: In double fertilisation the endosperm nucleus is
quiz.solution: One male nucleus fuses with two polar nuclei, giving a 3n endosperm.

quiz.q: After fertilisation the ovary of a flower develops into the
quiz.solution: The ovary wall becomes the pericarp of the fruit while ovules become seeds.

quiz.q: Fertilisation in humans normally occurs in the
quiz.solution: The sperm meets the ovum in the upper part of the Fallopian tube.

quiz.q: Ovulation in a regular 28-day menstrual cycle occurs around day
quiz.solution: An LH surge at mid-cycle releases the ovum from the Graafian follicle.

quiz.q: The hormone that maintains the uterine lining after ovulation is
quiz.solution: Progesterone from the corpus luteum keeps the endometrium thick and vascular.

quiz.q: The structure that allows exchange of materials between mother and fetus is the
quiz.solution: The placenta permits diffusion of gases, nutrients and wastes without mixing of blood.
The grasshopper passes through egg, nymph and adult stages with no pupa.

quiz.q: Vasectomy as a family planning method involves
options: cutting and tying the vas deferens
quiz.solution: The sperm ducts are cut so that semen contains no sperm; hormone production continues.
